item.title: East-West pairing plan bears fruit
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
East-West pairing plan bears fruit Cooperation between Fujian and Ningxia lifts thousands out of poverty Mabel Chinomona, president of the Senate of Zimbabwe, visited Northwest China's Ningxia Hui autonomous region in July, a trip she described as "valuable" as she got to witness first-hand one of the most remarkable success stories of poverty alleviation and rural transformation in contemporary history. During the tour, Chinomona, who is also a Political Bureau member and secretary of the Women's League of ZANU-PF, the African nation's ruling party, visited a paddy-fish ecological park, a green energy supply station and a coal-based new materials technology company. "The achievements we have witnessed in Ningxia provide practical evidence of the effectiveness of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, particularly its emphasis on people-centered development and the pursuit of common prosperity," Chinomona said. What impressed her the most was the partnership between Southeast China's Fujian province and Ningxia, which has become one of China's most celebrated examples of East-West paired assistance in poverty alleviation. In 1996, the Communist Party of China Central Committee launched a program to promote poverty alleviation cooperation between the more developed eastern region and the less-developed western region, as part of a broader national strategy to narrow regional development gaps and promote common prosperity. Under this program, Ningxia and Fujian were paired together. President Xi Jinping, then deputy secretary of the CPC Fujian Provincial Committee, oversaw the progress of the cooperation. Under his leadership, the two regions took the lead in establishing a joint conference mechanism and initiating mutual exchanges of officials through temporary assignments. This cooperation gave birth to Minning township, the name combining the Chinese abbreviations for Fujian, which is "Min", and Ningxia, which is "Ning". Thanks to the sustained efforts of officials and residents of both regions, what was once a desolate wasteland is today a prosperous township of 66,000 people, where as of 2025, relocated residents boasted a per capita disposable income of more than 20,000 yuan ($2,945). By 2020, all 803,000 impoverished people in the autonomous region had been lifted out of poverty. With China entering a new phase of high-quality development, Fujian-Ningxia cooperation is moving steadily toward higher-quality growth. "These achievements illustrate how visionary leadership, targeted poverty alleviation, industrial policy and environmental sustainability can work together to deliver lasting prosperity for the people," said Chinomona. For Zimbabwe, she said, these experiences offer invaluable lessons. "The success story of Ningxia inspires us to explore innovative models that can be adapted to our own circumstances, particularly in rural communities where sustainable livelihoods remain central to our national development agenda," she added. This year marks the 30th anniversary of the East-West pairing assistance program. In June, President Xi made instructions on steadily advancing cooperation between China's eastern and western regions, urging further efforts to boost coordinated regional development and secure solid progress in advancing common prosperity for all. He called for efforts to draw on and apply the valuable experience gained from the cooperation between Fujian and Ningxia, refine the cooperation mechanisms, and broaden the scope of cooperation. It is important to promote industrial complementarity, personnel exchanges, mutual learning in technology, sharing of ideas, and mutual learning in work styles between the eastern and western regions, thereby achieving mutual benefit, win-win outcomes and common development, Xi said. Yaomo, once an impoverished mountain village in Guyuan city, Ningxia, has undergone a remarkable transformation. "With government-provided preferential loans and subsidies, the villagers ventured into the cool-season vegetable industry. Under the guidance of resident agricultural experts, the vegetable industry has thrived, and our incomes have steadily increased," said Guo Shaoling, a farmer from the village. Guo said that local government also supported the villagers by establishing an online sales plat-form for agricultural products, helping them navigate market risks. "With this comprehensive support system, the vegetable industry has evolved from simple greenhouse farming to a full-fledged industrial chain." In the past, the village's poverty drove young people to seek opportunities elsewhere. However, the success of the vegetable industry has drawn many of them back. "Now, more and more young people are returning to join us in cultivating vegetables and developing the industry. The once-struggling village is now a thriving community, full of hope and opportunity," Guo said. Mohammed Ouzzine, vice-president of the House of Representatives of Morocco, said China's comprehensive governance model for poverty alleviation has left a deep impression on him. A significant amount of fiscal resources has been mobilized to support poverty alleviation projects, and a package of innovative measures has been implemented, including developing industry, relocating people, promoting education and improving the social security network, Ouzzine observed. Noting that poverty is a common challenge faced by all of humanity, he called for strengthening international cooperation on poverty reduction. Ghulom Halimzoda, chairman of the Socialist Party of Tajikistan, said the core lesson from China's experience in reducing poverty is to uphold the people-centered development philosophy, which is of utmost importance. The journey of Chinese modernization and the development path of Tajikistan both powerfully demonstrate that as long as a nation remains focused on the well-being of the people and progresses steadily, the goals, no matter how ambitious they are, can eventually be met, he said.

item.title: US criticism of Starbucks in Xinjiang rejected
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
US criticism of Starbucks in Xinjiang rejected China has firmly rejected criticism from a US congressional committee regarding Starbucks' expansion into the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. Beijing stressed that the move of the US consumer giant demonstrates the region's social stability and economic vitality as more domestic and international brands tap its growing consumer market. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Saturday that claims of so-called genocide in Xinjiang are "a blatant lie", in response to a question about criticism from the US House Select Committee on China, which had described Starbucks' decision to open stores in the region as "morally bankrupt". "Relevant US institutions are accustomed to fabricating issues and attacking and smearing China for political purposes, and have no credibility whatsoever," Guo said. "Xinjiang today enjoys social stability, economic development, ethnic unity and religious harmony," he added. "China will continue to expand high-standard opening-up and provide more opportunities for foreign companies to invest and operate in China." Starbucks opened its first two stores in Xinjiang on Sept 29, both in Urumqi, the regional capital — one at the city's Grand Bazaar and the other at Urumqi Tianshan International Airport. The openings marked the global coffee chain's debut in the region and its latest expansion in China, its second-largest market after the US. The Grand Bazaar flagship store incorporates local elements into its design, including Atlas silk, ethnic musical instruments and bazaar-inspired architecture. The airport outlet adopts a "silk road station" concept to serve travelers at the regional transport hub. Both locations feature locally inspired offerings. During the weeklong National Day holiday, a Xinjiang-inspired drink and three food items are also being offered at more than 2,700 Starbucks stores across 41 Chinese cities, bringing the region's flavors to consumers nationwide. "Entering Xinjiang is not only about further expanding our store network, but also gives us an opportunity to go deeper into this vibrant market and build long-term connections with consumers here," said Molly Liu, CEO of Starbucks China, adding that the company would continue to deepen its presence in Xinjiang and develop stores, products and experiences tailored to local demand. Starbucks is not alone in looking to the region for growth. Domestic giant Luckin Coffee opened its first 11 self-operated stores in Urumqi in May 2024, while Cotti Coffee had entered the Xinjiang market earlier through its franchise model. The expansion of major coffee brands comes alongside strong growth in Xinjiang's tourism sector. The region received 323 million tourist visits in 2025, up 8 percent year-on-year, with tourism spending rising 8.4 percent in the same period to 370 billion yuan ($52 billion), according to regional government data. Retail sales have also returned to growth this year. Xinjiang's retail sales of consumer goods reached 263.03 billion yuan in the first eight months of 2026, up 0.3 percent year-on-year, after declining 0.3 percent in the first seven months, official data showed. The region's broader corporate base is also expanding. Xinjiang had 2,647 registered foreign-invested enterprises by the end of June, up 6.91 percent from a year earlier, while the total number of registered market entities reached 2.73 million, according to regional market regulators. Nationwide, China saw 35,000 newly established foreign-invested enterprises in the first half of 2026, up 7 percent year-on-year, according to the State Administration for Market Regulation. The number of newly established foreign-invested enterprises in wholesale and retail rose 11.9 percent.

item.title: Chinese carmakers drive Australia's electric shift
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Chinese carmakers drive Australia's electric shift The Everything Electric Sydney trade show arrived with the Australian spring this year. The Southern Hemisphere's largest event of its kind, the home energy and electric vehicle show has become a major stage for Chinese carmakers. Industry data showed that battery EV sales in Australia broke records in August, surging 171 percent year-on-year and accounting for nearly one-fourth of all new vehicle sales that month. Five Chinese brands — BYD, GWM, MG, Geely and Chery — sold more than 26,000 vehicles combined, claiming five of the top 10 spots in Australia's auto market. At the show, held from Sept 18 to 20, I met Anthony Crawford, cofounder of automotive review platform CarExpert. He said Chinese cars were dominating Australian new vehicle sales for good reason. "They provide the technology. They provide the design, now getting so good," Crawford said. The Chinese auto industry has been a game changer and deserves credit for helping accelerate EV growth in Australia, he added. Another trend being driven by Chinese cars also caught his attention. After seeing a new model from a Chinese carmaker, he was particularly impressed by its AI features. Instead of using "broken English" or simple commands, drivers can speak to the car more like a normal conversation, which he found very convenient. Bringing AI into cars, Crawford said, was another game-changing development for the Chinese auto industry. Australia is a vast country, where driving conditions can shift quickly from city streets to the outback. Range, charging, and a vehicle's ability to handle different road conditions are practical concerns for car buyers. Easing "range anxiety" while meeting diverse driving needs has become an important test of whether a car brand can truly serve the local market. At the show, I met a car enthusiast who had come to see the latest models from Chinese carmakers. He said he has a fleet of 20 to 30 cars and also works in the auto industry. He frequently travels around Australia, sometimes covering long distances where fuel stations can be few and far between. He hopes a hybrid can handle everyday city driving while also performing well when he heads into the outback or even the desert. "I think they are just being smart. They are looking at what consumers want and providing the right product," he said. In March, I attended an event held by the Australian Automotive Dealer Association. In a speech at the gathering, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described buying a car as "one of the biggest financial decisions Australians make". Buying a car is often tied to important moments in life, such as welcoming a new baby or starting a new job, he said. In this respect, Australians and Chinese are actually quite similar. That is also why entering a new market means much more for a carmaker than simply shipping cars in and putting them on display. Price, design, driving range, safety, after-sales service and how well a vehicle fits the local way of life can all shape a consumer's choice. For carmakers, gaining a foothold in a mature market like Australia also raises another question: Beyond the design and quality Chinese cars are already known for, what new technologies could take the industry to its next stage? Chery offered one possible answer at the Sydney show by bringing its newly developed humanoid robot, Mornine, to the exhibition. A company executive told me that the robot grew out of practical needs in Chery's overseas business, including dealership operations and multilingual services. The company hopes to apply the technology, talent, manufacturing expertise and supply chain capabilities it has developed in the auto industry to new fields. Official data showed that car purchases in Australia rose 10.3 percent in the second quarter of this year, even as spending in most other categories remained weak. EVs were an important driver of that growth, helping lift household consumption and, in turn, economic growth. So, will the next generation of products from China help drive a new wave of consumption in Australia? We will have to wait and see. The author is chief correspondent at China Daily Asia-Pacific Bureau based in Sydney.

item.title: VPP network powers up as nation eyes smarter grid
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
VPP network powers up as nation eyes smarter grid Cutting-edge tech like IoT, AI to enhance stability, demand management China is accelerating a historic transformation of its massive electricity network, shifting away from a traditional model where power generation passively adjusts to meet demand, and toward a highly intelligent, interactive ecosystem that synchronizes generation, power grids, user loads and energy storage. As the country's renewable energy installations break records at a breathtaking pace, industry experts and policymakers increasingly view the demand side as the next great frontier for ensuring grid stability and achieving the nation's ambitious decarbonization goals. The recently released 15th Five-Year Plan for New Power System Construction (2026-30) outlines this paradigm shift. The blueprint targets a maximum regulation capacity of over 50 gigawatts for virtual power plants (VPPs) by 2030, establishing them as a crucial vehicle for demand-side grid interaction. Furthermore, the plan mandates the high-level absorption of over 2.8 billion kilowatts of renewable energy by the end of the decade. Unlike conventional facilities defined by physical generators and smokestacks, a VPP is an advanced, cloud-based digital aggregator. Powered by the internet of things, big data and artificial intelligence, a VPP links and orchestrates thousands of decentralized energy assets — including rooftop solar arrays, battery storage units and electric vehicle charging networks. During periods of peak demand or fluctuating renewable output, the platform can remotely discharge stored power or throttle back consumption in real time, delivering the same grid-balancing capabilities as a traditional peaking power station, but at a fraction of the capital cost and with zero additional carbon emissions. This structural pivot is born of necessity. As of the end of June, China's cumulative installed capacity of wind and solar power reached 1.95 billion kW, accounting for roughly 48.3 percent of the country's total power generation capacity, according to the National Energy Administration. However, relying heavily on wind and solar means the power supply is increasingly at the mercy of the weather. "While our green power capacity continues to set new global benchmarks, its inherent weather-dependent traits are becoming glaringly obvious," said Peng Yuehui, deputy director of the scientific and technological research institute at North China Electric Power University. "Power generation fluctuates significantly, and extreme weather can trigger 'roller-coaster' style volatility in daily power supply and demand," said Peng. Peng cited a major new energy base in Northwest China as an example. During peak sunlight hours at noon, the facility frequently has to curtail its output by 30 percent due to a lack of immediate demand or transmission capacity. Conversely, during the evening load peak when the sun sets, the grid faces a 40 percent power deficit. "The traditional power system operating model is simply no longer sustainable. The intermittency, randomness and volatility of renewable energy pose immense challenges to grid stability, demanding far higher levels of systemic flexibility," Peng added. Zhang Jieqing, chief representative of the Natural Resources Defense Council Beijing office, echoed this sentiment, noting that the speed of building system regulation capacity has severely lagged behind the explosive growth of wind and solar installations. "The spatial and temporal mismatch between supply and demand has always existed," Zhang said. "When renewable penetration was low, the grid could balance itself internally. But as green power becomes the dominant source, relying solely on traditional supply-side adjustments cannot solve the root problem." A report released earlier by the NRDC revealed that China's green commitment and rapidly developing new energy industry are fast-tracking the development of VPPs. As renewable energy makes up an ever-larger share of the power grid, mounting pressure on system flexibility and grid reliability is spurring demand for clean, agile and economically viable new market participants, it said. Compounding this is the steady growth of new electricity demand. The rapid proliferation of EVs and energy-intensive AI data centers is adding immense pressure to the grid, often occurring during evening peak hours, which widens the peak-to-valley load difference. Faced with these bottlenecks, the industry consensus is clear: China must look beyond power plants and grid infrastructure to tap into the massive, idle regulatory resources on the user side. Lin Boqiang, head of the China Institute for Studies in Energy Policy at Xiamen University, noted that the era of relying purely on power generators and grid operators for flexibility is coming to an end. "For high-quality renewable energy development, we must adopt a holistic systems approach. By innovating market mechanisms and unlocking the potential of user-side resources and virtual power plants, we can build a new ecological loop for renewable energy absorption," Lin said. Initial estimates suggest that the combined regulation potential of commercial and industrial flexible loads, EVs and distributed storage exceeds 300 million kW — equivalent to the capacity of roughly 150 large-scale pumped-storage hydropower stations. However, because these resources are individually small, geographically scattered and possess vastly different response characteristics, traditional centralized grid dispatching cannot effectively manage them. Using advanced digitalization, IoT platforms and AI, VPPs aggregate distributed solar panels, energy storage systems and EV charging stations. They transform these fragmented assets into an "invisible power plant" that can be dispatched by the grid on demand. According to NEA data, China had built 470 VPP projects by the end of 2025, with a measured maximum regulation capacity of 16.85 million kW, forming one of the world's leading VPP clusters. Yet, there remains vast room for improvement. For comparison, Germany manages about 18 million kW of similar resources, but achieves a utilization rate of 65 percent in its mature projects, a benchmark China is actively striving to match through market reforms. Real-world applications are already demonstrating immense value. During the summer of 2025, Shanghai successfully executed the nation's first GW-scale VPP actual-measurement dispatch, successfully shaving 1.16 million kW off the city's peak load. Shanghai authorities have since clarified market entry mechanisms, allowing VPPs to participate directly in the electricity spot market, paving the way for sustainable commercial models, equitable profit distribution and cross-regional trading. Kang Chongqing, a professor at Tsinghua University, highlighted the transformative potential of data centers in this new paradigm. With computing loads projected to account for 8 to 10 percent of total societal power demand in the future, AI data centers will require over 1 billion kW of green power by 2060, he said. "By designing systems that allow computing tasks to essentially 'chase green electrons' — shifting processing workloads to regions and times when renewable energy is abundant — we can achieve a triple victory of reducing data center carbon footprints, helping the grid balance loads and synergistically lowering overall emissions," Kang said. While VPPs provide the digital software to manage distributed demand, utility-scale new energy storage provides the vital physical hardware to anchor the grid. In this arena, China continues to maintain the world's largest installed capacity, marking a historic transition for the technology from a supplementary role to a critical backbone. According to the China New Energy Storage Development Report (2026) issued by the NEA, the country's installed capacity of new energy storage reached a staggering 136 GW by the end of 2025. This represents an 84 percent year-on-year surge and a massive 40-fold expansion compared to the end of 2020.

item.title: Collections soar as film industry gets holiday boost
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Fueled by new releases and the National Day holiday, the Chinese film industry is experiencing a high with crowds surging to cinemas all over the country. As of Oct 4, the total box office collection for the year had surpassed 30.2 billion yuan ($4.5 billion), with the ongoing National Day holiday providing the latest push. Topping the holiday box office favorite list is director Chen Sicheng's crime drama Traces of Justice, adapted from real-life cases solved by Cui Daozhi, a recipient of the July 1 Medal and a renowned expert in firearms and ammunition trace identification. With actors Zhang Yi and Li Xuejian portraying the younger and older versions of Cui Xun — the protagonist based on Cui Daozhi's character — the film chronicles the development of China's criminal investigation technologies through four cases: the 1971 serial murders and sexual assaults of young girls' corpses, the 1983 brutal killing of three colleagues by a high-ranking official's son, the 1998 bus suicide bombing, and a 2016 serial rape and murder case. Chen revealed that he was recommended a book about Cui Daozhi four years ago, which prompted him to visit the expert's residence in Harbin, Heilongjiang province, in the summer of 2023. Hailed as China's Sherlock Holmes, Cui Daozhi, 92, has participated in the on-site investigation of over 1,000 cases and identified more than 7,000 pieces of trace and physical evidence without a single error. Following Traces of Justice, which has raked in 257 million yuan, in second place is fantasy comedy Mr. &Mrs. Pardon, which has star couple Xiao Shenyang and Shen Chunyang playing a couple on screen for the first time since their marriage over 20 years ago. The protagonists, on the verge of divorce, unexpectedly find their souls swapped — forcing them to live and work in each other's shoes and rediscover the meaning of marriage. The film, Shen's directorial debut, has grossed 151 million yuan. Two summer blockbusters, the war drama Once Upon a Time in the Middle East and the animated hit All Wishes Come True! are still going strong, securing the third and fifth highest-grossing spots on the list respectively. Peppa Pig: Perfect Holiday, which follows the pig family's unplanned trip to China, has become the fourth highest-grossing film of the holiday season. Helmed by Chinese director Liu Yuan, the film incorporates Chinese elements to resonate with local audiences, including scenes of the animals making dumplings and racing dragon boats. The National Day holiday has seen the box office haul surpass 700 million yuan, while related businesses — from cuisine to set-jetting — have also put up impressive shows. According to China Media Group, the total output value of the film industry chain is estimated to have exceeded 470 billion yuan since the beginning of this year. Cheng Fei, a Beijing-based industry observer, said the holiday has seen a new trend emerge: the market is no longer dominated by a single phenomenal hit. With the transformation of audience tastes and growing demand for diversity, the domestic film industry no longer expects a single blockbuster to appeal to all audiences. Instead, the approach is to segment the market — using different types of films to attract viewers from different backgrounds, said Cheng. That segmentation is visible in this year's lineup. Hong Kong crime drama fans can find a touch of nostalgia in Louis Koo's Mastermind; those drawn to feminist themes can explore Waiting for Myself; and Hollywood diehards have two options — Brad Pitt's survival thriller Heart of the Beast and the sci-fi horror Resident Evil. Despite facing challenges such as shrinking investment and the rise of artificial intelligence-generated content, China's film industry has demonstrated strong vitality and a determination to adapt, said industry analysts. As of the end of September, China had added 438 cinemas and 2,632 screens nationwide, bringing the total number of screens to nearly 96,000 — the highest in the world, according to the China Film Administration. With the proportion of newly added cinemas in county-level and township commercial districts continuing to rise, the trend indicates that the domestic film market is steadily expanding into lower-tier areas to reach a broader audience, analysts said.

item.title: From a tin of tea to Chinese champion
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
From a tin of tea to Chinese champion A German student's story of transformation showcases how learning Mandarin opened new horizons and opportunities, culminating in a prestigious global victory, Li Yingxue reports. When Levi Benjamin Petersen was in high school, the first Chinese character that truly caught his attention appeared on a tin of tea imported from China. It was fu, meaning good fortune. The German teenager did not know what it meant, but was fascinated by its intricate yet orderly structure. Why was it written this way? he wondered. Did Chinese words change with tense, as they did in German and English? Petersen could not speak Chinese then, nor could he have imagined that his fascination with a single character would begin a journey that would eventually take him to China. Years later, in a tea garden in Fuzhou, Fujian province, Petersen touched a tea plant for the first time. He learned to pick and process tea with local masters and the custom of tapping one's fingers on the table to express thanks when tea is poured. Days later, Petersen stood on the top podium at the global finals of the 25th "Chinese Bridge" Chinese Proficiency Competition for Foreign College Students in Xiamen, Fujian, where he was named the overall champion.

item.title: Smart machines transform China's farms
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Smart machines transform China's farms Editor's note: A new wave of technological innovation is sweeping across China's agricultural landscape. From intelligent harvesters to agricultural robots and artificial intelligence-powered drones, cutting-edge farm machinery is transforming farming practices in the country. Equipped with high-precision positioning, machine vision, AI and real-time data systems, these machines are making farming more precise, automated and data-driven. These innovations are reshaping agriculture, with intelligent machines playing an increasingly important role alongside land and crops. China Daily reporter Zhao Yimeng will walk you through these pieces of equipment. GEAIR Intelligent Breeding Robot The world's first intelligent breeding robot, GEAIR automates cross-pollination with remarkable precision. Using deep-learning technology, it identifies flowers and performs precision pollination. The system combines biotechnology, AI and robotics, allowing it to patrol fields continuously and perform pollination round the clock. This reduces the labor and time required for conventional manual breeding. In tomato hybrid breeding, it shortens the breeding cycle from five years to just one year and reduces labor costs by over 25 percent. In soybean breeding, it reduces manual pollination time by 76.2 percent, automating a traditionally labor-intensive process. Source: Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

item.title: Young riders' grit on tracks
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Young riders' grit on tracks Youth motocross builds resilience and discipline amid growing popularity At the 2026 FIM World Superbike Championship, Chinese motorcycle startup ZXMOTO secured five historic wins, drawing global attention to the rapid rise of China's motorcycle racing prowess. On Beijing's off-road tracks, young riders chase their dreams amid dust and engine roars, learning resilience through falls and forging strength at high speed. They emerge as the inspiring new generation in China's youth motocross scene. Xuanxuan, a third-grade pupil, began motocross training at six on a 50cc motorcycle. Four years of rigorous weekend training taught him corner control, obstacle navigation and jump techniques. "Flying over that jump makes me feel so free; it makes all the hard work worthwhile," he says. Although he had cried minutes earlier after spraining his ankle, he lit up when talking about what he loves.

item.title: Serving up an ace cultural experience
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Serving up an ace cultural experience Stars immerse themselves in Beijing's traditional, and trendy, activities A trip without a dip into the profound culture is never a complete China Open experience, and tennis' top stars are enjoying a break from the grueling season to soak up Beijing's rich history and tradition. With world-class facilities, top services and highest prize money in Asia on offer, the China Open never disappoints when it comes to delivering a major-caliber tournament experience for the glittering cast of men's and women's stars it attracts every year. It's the incomparable "Beijing Experience", though, that sets it apart from the others in the same category, with international players presented with cultural experience trips or events to explore the Chinese capital's timeless heritage, folk customs and modern trends. It's a treat that suits 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic perfectly, with the Serbian great, known for his inner strength and serenity when facing fierce on-court battles, rejuvenated after a pre-tournament visit to the Summer Palace, an imperial park in the northwestern Beijing suburbs known for its ancient grandeur and tranquility. After taking a walk around the Kunming Lake to savor the serene ambiance of the park, Djokovic spent some time experiencing two quintessential Chinese traditions. First, he tried his hand at water calligraphy by learning how to write the Chinese characters of his name with a big brush pen on the ground.

item.title: Nation tops Asian Games table for 12th time
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Nation tops Asian Games table for 12th time China retained the top spot for a record 12th consecutive time as the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games drew to a close on Sunday, creating another record with the number of gold medals won and introducing to the world a new generation of promising Chinese athletes. The Chinese competitors won 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals, a total haul of 341 medals, surpassing the previous record of 165 golds won in an overseas Asian Games set in 2006 at Doha, Qatar. Japan finished second with 83 golds, followed by the Republic of Korea with 39. Beyond the medal haul, the Games also provided a platform for a new generation of sporting talents. China's 13-year-old swimming sensation Yu Zidi was named the Most Valuable Player among females, while Thailand's 20-year-old sprinter Puripol Boonson won in the men's category. Yu won gold in all three of her individual events, setting Games records in each, including an Asian record. Boonson completed a sprint double, winning the men's 100m in a Games record of 9.90 seconds and the 200m in 19.88, equaling the Asian record. "Tonight, we close a Games that will shape the next generation of Asian sport," Olympic Council of Asia President Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani said in his closing ceremony speech. Athletes set 54 world records and 89 Asian records during the Games, OCA Director General Husain Al Musallam said. He said the Games had continued to unite Asia through sport despite conflicts and economic instability around the world. "Asia is united in sport, in peace and in solidarity," he said. "This is our aim."
